# 2 Maccabees Chapter 4 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** The same Simon who had informed on the temple treasury now turned around and slandered Onias — spreading the story that Onias himself had set up the whole Heliodorus affair and had been behind the trouble from the start.

**2** He had the nerve to call a man who was a genuine benefactor of the city, a defender of his own people, and a devoted champion of the law — an enemy of the state.

**3** His hatred went so far that some of Simon's henchmen began committing murders.

**4** Onias could see where this was heading. He recognized that Apollonius son of Menestheus, governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was actively feeding Simon's malice.

**5** So he made his way to the king — not to bring charges against his own countrymen, but out of genuine concern for the welfare of all the people, both public and private.

**6** He could see clearly that without royal intervention, there would be no end to the turmoil, and Simon would never stop his madness.

**7** But then Seleucus died, and Antiochus — the one called Epiphanes — took the throne. Jason, the brother of Onias, bought his way into the high priesthood.

**8** His opening bid to the king: three hundred and sixty talents of silver, plus another eighty from a secondary revenue source.

**9** On top of that, he promised a hundred and fifty more in exchange for permission to establish a gymnasium and an athletic club for young men, and to officially register Jerusalemites as citizens of Antioch.

**10** The king agreed. Jason took office — and immediately set about converting his fellow Jews to a Greek way of life.

**11** He swept aside the royal privileges that the Jews had won through John, father of Eupolemus, who had been sent on the mission to establish the Roman alliance. He abolished the traditional way of life and installed practices that violated the law.

**12** With great enthusiasm he built a gymnasium right under the shadow of the citadel and recruited the finest young men of Jerusalem to wear the Greek broad-brimmed hat.

**13** Hellenization reached its peak under Jason. The man was godless — no true high priest — and his wickedness drove the tide of foreign customs to flood in.

**14** The priests couldn't be bothered with their duties at the altar anymore. They despised the sanctuary, they skipped the sacrifices, and the moment the discus thrower called the athletes to the track, they were off to the wrestling grounds — taking part in activities the law expressly forbade.

**15** Everything their ancestors had held sacred — they treated as worthless. Greek prestige was all that mattered to them.

**16** The disaster that came upon them afterward was entirely of their own making. Those very people whose lifestyle they had copied so eagerly turned out to be the ones who punished them.

**17** To act with contempt toward the laws of God is no small matter. What came after made that devastatingly clear.

**18** While the five-year games were being held at Tyre in the presence of the king,

**19** that despicable man Jason sent envoys to attend as spectators — carrying three hundred silver drachmas as a contribution to the sacrifice to Hercules. But even the messengers who carried the money felt uncomfortable with it. They decided it would be wrong to use these funds for a pagan sacrifice.

**20** So the money Jason had specifically earmarked for Hercules' sacrifice was rerouted — by the bearers' own decision — to fund the construction of warships.

**21** When Apollonius son of Menestheus was dispatched to Egypt for the coronation of King Philometor, Antiochus discovered that Philometor had turned against him. He grew concerned about his own position and traveled to Joppa, then continued on to Jerusalem.

**22** Jason and the city put on an elaborate reception for him — torchlight processions, cheering crowds, a magnificent welcome — after which Antiochus led his army on into Phoenicia.

**23** Three years later, Jason sent Menelaus — brother of that same Simon — up to the king to deliver the money and to handle some other pressing business.

**24** But once Menelaus was standing before the king, he sized up the opportunity and outbid Jason for the high priesthood by three hundred talents of silver. He walked away with the commission.

**25** He came back to Jerusalem with the royal authorization — but with none of the character that office required. He had the heart of a tyrant and the temper of a wild beast.

**26** Jason, who had pushed his own brother out to grab the position, now found himself pushed out in turn — forced to flee as a refugee into Ammonite territory.

**27** Menelaus held onto the office, but he never paid the king what he had promised.

**28** Sostratus, the commander of the citadel, kept pressing him for it — it was his job to collect the revenues. Eventually both men were hauled before the king.

**29** Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus in charge as his substitute; Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cyprian garrison.

**30** While all of this was going on, the people of Tarsus and Mallus rose in revolt — angry that their cities had been handed over as a gift to Antiochis, the king's mistress.

**31** The king rushed off to deal with it, leaving a senior official named Andronicus as his regent.

**32** Menelaus saw his chance. He handed over to Andronicus several golden vessels from the temple treasury — pieces he had already started selling off to dealers in Tyre and nearby cities.

**33** When Onias got word of what was happening, he raised the alarm — but he had already taken refuge in the protected sanctuary at Daphne, near Antioch.

**34** Menelaus pulled Andronicus aside and pushed him to have Onias killed. Andronicus went to Onias and extended a handshake, swore solemn oaths, and talked Onias into coming out of the sanctuary despite his misgivings. The moment Onias stepped out, Andronicus murdered him — without a thought for justice.

**35** The reaction was immediate and widespread. Not just Jews — people from many other nations were furious and appalled at this cold-blooded killing of an innocent man.

**36** When the king returned from Cilicia, the Jews of the city — along with sympathetic Greeks — put their case before him. They were grief-stricken that Onias had been murdered without any justification whatsoever.

**37** Antiochus was genuinely moved. He grieved, and he wept, thinking of the dignity and restraint that had marked the dead man's life.

**38** His grief turned to fury. He had Andronicus stripped of his purple robe right there and then, tore the garments off him, and marched him through the entire city to the very spot where Onias had been killed. There he had him executed. The LORD gave that murderer exactly what he deserved.

**39** Meanwhile, Lysimachus — with Menelaus's blessing — had been committing acts of sacrilege all over the city. When word of this spread, the people rose up against him. By this point a large number of golden vessels had already disappeared.

**40** As the crowds surged with anger, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and launched an attack — a brutal, unjustified assault, led by a man named Auranus who was as old as he was foolish.

**41** The people fought back with whatever they could grab: stones, wood, fistfuls of ash from the ground nearby. They hurled everything at Lysimachus's men in a chaotic volley.

**42** They wounded many, killed some, and sent the rest running. The temple plunderer himself they killed right beside the treasury.

**43** The council brought charges against Menelaus over the whole affair.

**44** When the king came to Tyre, three envoys sent by the council appeared before him to lay out the case.

**45** Menelaus could see that conviction was nearly certain. So he bribed Ptolemy son of Dorymenes with a large sum of money to lobby the king on his behalf.

**46** Ptolemy drew the king aside into a covered walkway, supposedly for a private word, and worked on him until he changed his mind.

**47** Menelaus — the man responsible for all the trouble — was cleared of every charge. The three envoys, who would have walked free before the most barbarous court imaginable, were condemned to death.

**48** The men who had stood up for their city, their villages, and the sacred vessels received nothing but an unjust death sentence.

**49** Even the Tyrians were sickened by it. Out of sheer disgust at the crime, they gave the three men a proper burial at their own expense.

**50** Menelaus stayed in power, kept there by the greed of the men who held authority over him. He grew worse with each passing day, the chief enemy of his own people.
